Matt Pocock is still a nice guy with reasonable opinions and shares a lot with us. I've personally learned from reading his skills.
Exposure is still valuable. Eventually you recognise a nice... ahem... opinion... just by looking at it. (Reply defending the value of reading others' shared skill sets, even if workflow-specific.)
Productivity suites of skills like this get shared as if they were innovations everyone can benefit from, when they're really extremely specific to that dev and their workflow. Everyone has one.

Skills are hardly transferrable unless you focus on globally applicable things like syntax and structure. The most useful skills are project- or organization-specific, the 'tribal knowledge' of coding.

All this could be one moderately-sized AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, and much of it doesn't need detail. Just write 'always follow TDD'. Skills are for calling scripts, adding specific data, or truly bespoke workflows. Detailing something like TDD probably hampers the model with a less accurate definition than it learned in training.

It's easier to build instructions as you go, learning from each time the bot stumbles. Starting with preset banks never works out long term. It's unsettling to catch the agent behaving oddly and realize it took a cue from imported instructions you never wrote, like playing pretend with someone else's rules.

The second skill's before/after example claims 'There's a problem with the materialization cascade' reads easier than 'There's a problem when a lesson inside a section of a course is made real (given a spot in the file system)'. Commenter preferred the original, plainer version.
Reply to the jargon complaint: it makes sense when you look at the CONTEXT.md file it refers to. It explicitly declares jargon so you don't need to redescribe the same thing every time.

Critic says Pocock takes a hand-wavy approach to engineering in a silo, mostly with Claude, then promotes the output as the best way on YouTube. The prose in the skills often has little utility; he should at least run SKILL.md files (e.g. wayfinder) through an impartial LLM to strip cruft and noise.
Commenter mocked the author's tendency to overcomplicate things, saying he needs something that stops him whenever he overcomplicates.
